chunks.title: Customer Acquisition — H2Ops
chunks.text: Customer Acquisition H2Ops Revenue & Growth AI-powered sales intelligence and customer acquisition automation. Sales Strategy AI Automation Revenue Growth

chunks.title: Customer Acquisition — what it is
chunks.text: An AI-assisted customer acquisition system that combines market research, prospect intelligence, personalized demonstrations, intelligent outreach and automated follow-ups to help businesses identify and engage potential customers more effectively.

chunks.title: Customer Acquisition — challenges
chunks.text: Sales teams waste time researching unsuitable prospects. Generic outreach struggles to communicate relevant value. Manual prospecting limits sales capacity. Inconsistent follow-ups result in missed opportunities. Fragmented customer information reduces pipeline visibility.

chunks.title: Customer Acquisition — value
chunks.text: Better allocation of sales resources. More relevant and personalized customer engagement. Reduced repetitive prospecting work. More consistent follow-up and opportunity management. A more scalable customer acquisition process.

chunks.title: Customer Acquisition — contribution
chunks.text: I worked across the commercial logic and the demo/follow-up layer, from defining who to target to connecting demo engagement with the next sales action. Problem: Generic outreach made it difficult for a prospect to see how the offer applied to their business, while the team needed replies and bookings to drive the next step. What I did: Defined the target segments, qualification criteria and follow-up rules used to prioritize prospects. Built parts of the H2Ops demo follow-up engine, including inbox sync and booking detection, and set up the contractor demo interface. Scope: I worked across strategy and implementation within a wider H2Ops acquisition workflow that also included lead sourcing, enrichment and outreach.

chunks.title: Customer Acquisition — process overview
chunks.text: A connected sales process from target definition to pipeline visibility. Replies and bookings can happen during initial outreach or later follow-up.

chunks.title: Customer Acquisition — Define the target customer
chunks.text: Define the target customer Identify the ideal customer. Define the ideal customer based on industry, location, company characteristics and business needs. This establishes where the sales team should focus its resources.

chunks.title: Customer Acquisition — Find new prospects
chunks.text: Find new prospects Discover potential buyers. Identify businesses that match the target customer profile, creating a structured list of potential sales opportunities without relying exclusively on manual research.

chunks.title: Customer Acquisition — Improve existing prospect data
chunks.text: Improve existing prospect data Identify who to contact. Improve existing company records by identifying decision-makers, contact information and relevant business details, while reducing incomplete or duplicate records.

chunks.title: Customer Acquisition — Prioritize opportunities
chunks.text: Prioritize opportunities Focus on promising prospects. Evaluate prospects against the target profile and available business signals, such as relevant hiring activity, to determine which opportunities warrant greater attention.

chunks.title: Customer Acquisition — AI-powered demonstrations
chunks.text: AI-powered demonstrations Show personalized business value. Generate personalized demonstration websites and AI experiences based on the prospect’s business, helping them understand how the proposed solution could work in their own environment.

chunks.title: Customer Acquisition — Intelligent outreach
chunks.text: Intelligent outreach Create relevant sales messages. Use business information and prospect context to prepare personalized messages that communicate relevant value rather than relying on generic sales pitches.

chunks.title: Customer Acquisition — Nurturing & follow-ups
chunks.text: Nurturing & follow-ups Adapt to customer engagement. Adapt subsequent communication based on demo activity, engagement and responses. Avoid unnecessary follow-ups when a prospect replies or books.

chunks.title: Customer Acquisition — Replies & bookings
chunks.text: Replies & bookings Capture sales opportunities. Identify replies and scheduled appointments so promising conversations can be handed to the sales team and the appropriate next action can be recorded.

chunks.title: Customer Acquisition — CRM & pipeline management
chunks.text: CRM & pipeline management Maintain sales visibility. Centralize prospect information, outreach history, engagement and opportunity status. Give the sales team a clearer understanding of where prospects stand and what requires attention.

chunks.title: Dispatch — H2Ops Dispatch
chunks.text: Dispatch H2Ops Dispatch Business & Operations A service operations platform connecting customer demand with contractor supply through coordinated matching, communication and booking management. Supply & Demand Coordination Operations Automation Service Management

chunks.title: Dispatch — what it is
chunks.text: A service operations platform designed for businesses that connect customers with independent service providers. The system combines customer intake, contractor acquisition and onboarding, service coverage, job matching, communication and booking confirmation into a coordinated operational process. Its objective is to help businesses manage both sides of a service marketplace while reducing manual coordination and improving operational visibility.

chunks.title: Dispatch — challenges
chunks.text: Time-consuming manual coordination between customers and contractors. Difficulty identifying suitable and available service providers. Fragmented communication and inconsistent follow-ups. Limited visibility into contractor readiness and service coverage. Customer requests becoming delayed or unresolved. Difficulty scaling operations without increasing administrative workload.

chunks.title: Dispatch — value
chunks.text: More efficient coordination of supply and demand. Reduced administrative and operational workload. Better utilization of contractor networks. Greater visibility into service requests and their progression. More consistent customer and contractor experiences. A more scalable service delivery model.

chunks.title: Dispatch — contribution
chunks.text: I worked on the front door of the dispatch process: how a service request enters the system and how the customer receives a reference. Problem: A request creates an expectation, but dispatch can only fulfil it when coverage, contractor readiness and availability line up. What I did: Built and refined the public intake flow: which request details dispatch receives, how the request is validated, and how the customer receives a confirmation reference. Scope: I worked on the intake-to-queue handoff; coverage, contractor activation and offer/confirmation sat within the wider Dispatch system.

chunks.title: Dispatch — process overview
chunks.text: Customer demand and contractor supply converge at matching, then move through communication and booking, with a secondary path for exceptions.

chunks.title: Dispatch — Customer request
chunks.text: Customer request Understand what the customer needs. Customers submit a service request describing the work they need, their location and relevant preferences. This creates a structured starting point for the business instead of relying on scattered messages or phone conversations.

chunks.title: Dispatch — Assess requirements
chunks.text: Assess requirements Understand the job requirements. Organize the customer’s request into actionable information, including the type of service, job scope, location and scheduling requirements. This helps the business understand what kind of contractor is needed.

chunks.title: Dispatch — Check service coverage
chunks.text: Check service coverage Determine whether demand can be served. Evaluate whether the business has suitable service coverage for the customer’s location and requirements. Requests outside current coverage can help identify opportunities for contractor recruitment and future market expansion.

chunks.title: Dispatch — Contractor acquisition
chunks.text: Contractor acquisition Expand the service provider network. Identify and recruit contractors based on the services and geographic markets the business wants to support. This helps align contractor acquisition with actual or anticipated customer demand.

chunks.title: Dispatch — Contractor onboarding
chunks.text: Contractor onboarding Understand each contractor’s capabilities. Collect relevant contractor information, including offered services, geographic coverage, availability and operating preferences. Structured contractor profiles provide the information needed to identify suitable service providers.

chunks.title: Dispatch — Contractor activation
chunks.text: Contractor activation Establish contractor readiness. Distinguish contractors who are potential partners from those who are ready to receive service opportunities. This helps the business understand its usable service capacity rather than relying solely on the size of its contractor database.

chunks.title: Dispatch — Match supply & demand
chunks.text: Match supply & demand Connect the request with suitable contractors. Identify eligible contractors based on the customer’s service requirements, location and contractor readiness. This reduces manual searching and helps allocate available service capacity more effectively.

chunks.title: Dispatch — Coordinate communication
chunks.text: Coordinate communication Manage offers and responses. Coordinate communication between customers, contractors and the dispatch team. Contractors receive relevant opportunities and can respond, while the business tracks the progression of each request.

chunks.title: Dispatch — Confirm the booking
chunks.text: Confirm the booking Establish a clear service commitment. Track contractor acceptance and customer confirmation as distinct steps. This gives the business greater visibility into whether a service opportunity has progressed into a confirmed arrangement.

chunks.title: Dispatch — Exception management
chunks.text: Exception management Resolve requests that need attention. Identify requests that cannot progress because of unavailable contractors, expired offers, unanswered communications or coverage limitations. These requests can be reviewed, reassigned where appropriate or handled by the operations team.

chunks.title: Dispatch — Operations management
chunks.text: Operations management Maintain visibility across the business. Centralize customer requests, contractor profiles, communication and booking progression. Give the operations team a clearer understanding of current demand, available supply and outstanding operational decisions.

chunks.title: AI Customer Communications — H2Ops
chunks.text: AI Customer Communications H2Ops AI Solutions An AI-powered communication system that manages customer inquiries, conversational interactions, appointment scheduling and customer reactivation. Conversational AI Customer Experience Communication Automation

chunks.title: AI Customer Communications — what it is
chunks.text: An AI-powered customer communication system that combines intelligent inquiry management, conversational voice and SMS agents, appointment scheduling and customer reactivation. The system helps businesses respond to customer needs, capture opportunities and manage routine conversations while reducing dependence on manual intervention.

chunks.title: AI Customer Communications — challenges
chunks.text: Missed calls and unanswered customer inquiries. Slow response times resulting in missed opportunities. Repetitive conversations consuming employee time. Limited customer service availability outside business hours. Time-consuming manual appointment management. Underutilized customer databases. Fragmented communication across multiple channels.

chunks.title: AI Customer Communications — value
chunks.text: Faster and more consistent customer responses. Extended customer communication availability. Reduced administrative workload. Better utilization of existing customer databases. More efficient appointment management. Increased communication capacity without proportional staffing increases.

chunks.title: AI Customer Communications — contribution
chunks.text: I led the project end-to-end, from the initial communication problem through planning, implementation, testing and release. Problem: Slow or inconsistent responses were losing inquiries, while booking commitments needed to respect service duration and calendar availability. What I did: Defined the inquiry triage and appointment rules: how inquiries were captured, prioritized and routed, and when a voice or SMS response could offer or change a time. Built and tested the AI voice and SMS workflows, including booking, rescheduling and cancellation paths, then prepared the system for release. Scope: The voice, SMS and reactivation examples were separate workflows within one communication system; I owned the project from idea through shipping.

chunks.title: AI Customer Communications — process overview
chunks.text: Incoming inquiries and customer reactivation converge into a shared understanding stage, then branch into parallel voice and SMS conversations before next actions and CRM tracking.

chunks.title: AI Customer Communications — Incoming inquiries
chunks.text: Incoming inquiries Capture new customer interest. Collect incoming customer inquiries and relevant contact information, including the source of the inquiry where available. This helps businesses organize incoming demand and reduce the likelihood of overlooking potential opportunities.

chunks.title: AI Customer Communications — Customer reactivation
chunks.text: Customer reactivation Reconnect with existing prospects. Identify previous customers and inactive prospects who may still benefit from the business’s services. Initiate relevant conversations to uncover opportunities within the existing customer database instead of relying exclusively on new customer acquisition.

chunks.title: AI Customer Communications — Understand customer needs
chunks.text: Understand customer needs Qualify and prioritize inquiries. Evaluate the nature, intent and relevance of each inquiry. Determine what the customer needs and which communication or follow-up approach is appropriate, allowing the business to allocate attention more effectively.

chunks.title: AI Customer Communications — AI voice agent
chunks.text: AI voice agent Handle natural phone conversations. Enable customers to interact with an AI-powered voice receptionist capable of understanding inquiries and supporting routine customer interactions, including appointment-related requests. This reduces dependence on staff availability for routine telephone conversations.

chunks.title: AI Customer Communications — AI SMS agent
chunks.text: AI SMS agent Engage customers through text. Use conversational AI to interpret customer messages, provide relevant responses and continue interactions through SMS. Customers can communicate asynchronously while the business maintains a more consistent response process.

chunks.title: AI Customer Communications — Determine next action
chunks.text: Determine next action Turn conversations into decisions. Identify the appropriate next step based on the customer’s request, conversation and available information. This may involve answering a question, managing an appointment, continuing the conversation or identifying a need for human assistance.

chunks.title: AI Customer Communications — Appointment management
chunks.text: Appointment management Book, reschedule or cancel. Support appointment-related requests by checking calendar availability and managing bookings, rescheduling or cancellations. This reduces administrative work and helps customers complete routine scheduling tasks more conveniently.

chunks.title: AI Customer Communications — Follow-up & human handoff
chunks.text: Follow-up & human handoff Continue or escalate conversations. Identify conversations requiring additional attention and determine whether further communication or human involvement is appropriate. The objective is to prevent opportunities from being overlooked while recognizing the limits of automated communication.

chunks.title: AI Customer Communications — CRM & communication tracking
chunks.text: CRM & communication tracking Maintain customer interaction visibility. Organize customer information, inquiry status, communication history and appointment activity. Give the business a clearer understanding of ongoing conversations and outstanding customer needs.

chunks.title: B.R.A.I.N. — H2Ops Brain
chunks.text: B.R.A.I.N. H2Ops Brain AI Solutions An organizational knowledge system that transforms business documentation, operating procedures and institutional knowledge into accessible, AI-powered business intelligence. Knowledge Management Retrieval-Augmented Generation (RAG) Enterprise AI Adoption

chunks.title: B.R.A.I.N. — what it is
chunks.text: An AI-powered organizational knowledge system designed to help businesses centralize, organize and access internal knowledge. B.R.A.I.N. combines standard operating procedures, business documentation, playbooks and organizational memory with an AI knowledge assistant designed to retrieve relevant information and provide company-specific guidance. Its objective is to make organizational knowledge more accessible, actionable and useful across the business.

chunks.title: B.R.A.I.N. — challenges
chunks.text: Business knowledge scattered across multiple documents and platforms. Employees spending excessive time searching for information. Repeated questions consuming management time. Inconsistent execution of business procedures. Loss of institutional knowledge when employees leave. Time-consuming employee onboarding. Generic AI assistants lacking company-specific context.

chunks.title: B.R.A.I.N. — value
chunks.text: Centralized organizational intelligence. Faster access to relevant business information. More consistent execution of company procedures. Reduced dependence on individual employees’ knowledge. More efficient employee training and onboarding. Company-specific AI assistance. Better preservation of institutional knowledge.

chunks.title: B.R.A.I.N. — contribution
chunks.text: I worked across the knowledge structure and the assistant experience, from defining how guidance was organized to building onboarding, chat, playbooks and organizational memory. Problem: Knowledge was scattered across documents and platforms, slowing onboarding and making routine answers depend on whoever was available. What I did: Defined the operating-library structure and document-access boundaries for procedures, decisions and playbooks. Implemented the assistant’s onboarding and chat experience, including the organization-scoped path that retrieved available documents and memory, and added playbook and organizational-memory features. Scope: The operating library and retrieval prototype remained separate systems; I worked across their knowledge structure and the assistant experience.

chunks.title: B.R.A.I.N. — process overview
chunks.text: Organizational knowledge is captured, organized and maintained so the AI assistant can retrieve relevant context and support informed decisions. The library and retrieval prototype are complementary.

chunks.title: B.R.A.I.N. — Business documentation
chunks.text: Business documentation Capture how the business operates. Collect standard operating procedures, company policies, sales playbooks and operational guidelines. Transform scattered business documentation into a structured organizational resource.

chunks.title: B.R.A.I.N. — Organizational memory
chunks.text: Organizational memory Preserve business knowledge and experience. Document important decisions, established practices, business strategies and lessons learned. Preserve valuable institutional knowledge so that it does not remain exclusively with individual employees or managers.

chunks.title: B.R.A.I.N. — Organize business knowledge
chunks.text: Organize business knowledge Create a structured knowledge library. Organize business information into relevant categories, departments, procedures and playbooks. Establish a consistent structure that makes information easier to maintain, locate and understand.

chunks.title: B.R.A.I.N. — Maintain & update knowledge
chunks.text: Maintain & update knowledge Keep organizational information relevant. Track changes to business documentation and maintain updated procedures as the organization evolves. Help distinguish established operating practices from outdated information.

chunks.title: B.R.A.I.N. — Employee question
chunks.text: Employee question Ask questions in natural language. Allow employees to ask questions about company procedures, responsibilities, sales practices or operational requirements without manually searching through multiple documents.

chunks.title: B.R.A.I.N. — Retrieve relevant knowledge
chunks.text: Retrieve relevant knowledge Find the information that matters. Identify relevant passages within the assistant’s available knowledge sources based on the employee’s question. Retrieval-augmented generation helps provide company-specific context rather than relying exclusively on a general AI model’s knowledge.

chunks.title: B.R.A.I.N. — AI-powered business assistance
chunks.text: AI-powered business assistance Provide contextual business guidance. Generate responses grounded in retrieved organizational information, within the appropriate organizational access boundaries. Help employees understand procedures, locate relevant guidance and navigate business processes.

chunks.title: B.R.A.I.N. — Informed decisions & execution
chunks.text: Informed decisions & execution Turn knowledge into practical action. Help employees make better-informed decisions, follow established procedures and complete routine tasks with greater independence. The objective is to improve organizational consistency while reducing dependence on management for routine guidance.

chunks.title: Safiy — Contextual AI
chunks.text: Safiy Contextual AI Product & Innovation A local-first AI workplace assistant that transforms conversations, professional context and knowledge into intelligent assistance and business actions. Contextual AI Workplace Productivity Product Innovation

chunks.title: Safiy — what it is
chunks.text: Safiy is a local-first AI workplace assistant designed to capture conversations, organize professional knowledge, provide contextual assistance and support actions across connected applications. By combining meeting intelligence, knowledge retrieval, real-time AI assistance and application integrations, Safiy bridges the gap between workplace conversations and business execution. Its objective is to make AI a contextual part of everyday professional workflows rather than a separate tool users must repeatedly provide with information.

chunks.title: Safiy — challenges
chunks.text: Valuable information lost after meetings. Excessive time spent taking notes and preparing summaries. Difficulty retrieving information from previous conversations. Frequent switching between business applications. Manual execution of post-meeting administrative tasks. Generic AI assistants lacking relevant workplace context. Privacy concerns surrounding sensitive business conversations.

chunks.title: Safiy — value
chunks.text: Improved meeting productivity. Better retention and accessibility of business knowledge. Reduced post-meeting administrative workload. More informed professional conversations. Greater continuity between discussions and business actions. Reduced application switching. Greater control over sensitive information.

chunks.title: Safiy — contribution
chunks.text: I worked on the knowledge and release layer of Safiy, building on the open-source Meeting Transcriber project. Problem: Meeting context is easy to lose, but uploading recordings can create privacy and adoption barriers. What I did: Added Knowledge Bank imports, improved retrieval indexing and prepared beta releases. Scope: I worked within a local-first direction — recording and transcription on the Mac by default, with connected services treated as explicit choices. The broader assistant, connected actions and suggested tasks extend beyond the features I built.

chunks.title: Safiy — process overview
chunks.text: Conversations and connected knowledge create context for the assistant, which supports real-time help and business actions. Preserved knowledge feeds continuous intelligence back into future context.

chunks.title: Safiy — Capture conversations
chunks.text: Capture conversations Capture workplace discussions. Record and transcribe professional conversations across virtual and in-person meetings. Transform spoken information into searchable content that can be reviewed and used beyond the original conversation.

chunks.title: Safiy — Connect knowledge
chunks.text: Connect knowledge Bring relevant information together. Organize documents, reference materials, previous conversations and project-specific information through Knowledge Banks and Workspaces. Give the AI assistant access to relevant professional context rather than relying exclusively on general knowledge.

chunks.title: Safiy — Understand context
chunks.text: Understand context Identify relevant workplace information. Use conversation content, meeting history and available knowledge to establish context around the user’s current activity. Retrieve relevant information to support more meaningful assistance.

chunks.title: Safiy — Contextual AI assistant
chunks.text: Contextual AI assistant Provide intelligence around your work. Combine available professional context with AI capabilities to help users understand information, explore ideas, answer questions and identify potential next steps. Reduce the need to repeatedly explain the same business context to an AI assistant.

chunks.title: Safiy — Real-time assistance
chunks.text: Real-time assistance Support conversations as they happen. Provide contextual suggestions, relevant answers, preparation guidance and potential action recommendations during professional conversations. Help users remain focused and better informed without constantly switching between applications.

chunks.title: Safiy — Business action execution
chunks.text: Business action execution Turn discussions into business actions. Support actions across connected applications such as Gmail, Google Calendar, Google Docs, Sheets and Drive. Help translate meeting discussions into practical tasks, documents, email drafts and scheduled activities, subject to supported integrations and user permissions.

chunks.title: Safiy — Preserve workplace knowledge
chunks.text: Preserve workplace knowledge Retain valuable professional context. Organize meeting transcripts, conversation history and related information within accessible workspaces. Allow users to retrieve previous discussions and relevant knowledge without manually reconstructing past events.

chunks.title: Safiy — Continuous intelligence
chunks.text: Continuous intelligence Carry knowledge into future work. Make accumulated professional knowledge available to support future conversations, questions and activities. Create continuity between past discussions and present work while maintaining user control over stored information.

chunks.title: Entering the workforce — Entering
chunks.text: Entering the workforce Entering 2022–2023 H&M was my first real lesson in commercial cause and effect. A busy floor shows you immediately whether someone understood the customer: the product they were shown, the question that was asked, the reason they came back. I learned to read people, handle pressure and take responsibility for an experience I did not control. The job was not strategic, but it taught me where strategy eventually has to prove itself — in a customer’s decision. Retail taught me that performance is built in small, repeated interactions. It made me want to understand what turns a good conversation into a repeatable result — which led me into coaching. chunks.title: Discovering sales and leadership — Sales & Leadership
chunks.text: Discovering sales and leadership Sales & Leadership 2023–2024 As a Sales Coach, I stopped being measured only by my own numbers. I had to explain what good looked like, diagnose why someone was struggling and give people a way to improve that they could actually use. I built training materials, ran workshops for more than ten associates and held weekly conversations about goals and progress. Team sales improved by 15% over that period. The result mattered, but the more useful lesson was that performance is shaped by the system around a person: clarity, feedback, incentives and support. Coaching showed me that results scale through other people. It also exposed the limits of influencing a single store, which pushed me toward commercial roles with a wider view. Coaching Sales training Team development Performance conversations Customer relationships Sales training materials Workshops for 10+ associates Weekly goal and progress meetings

chunks.title: Developing commercial experience — Commercial
chunks.text: Developing commercial experience Commercial 2024–2026 At MPN Capital Markets, I learned to create a commercial conversation from nothing: research the market, qualify a prospect, find a reason to reach out and earn a response. I finished with the highest number of qualified leads in a two-week period. At Browns, the feedback loop was shorter and more personal. I sold over $400,000 individually by reading budget, taste and intent — and by being direct enough to help someone decide. The product mattered; understanding the person mattered more. Together, the two roles moved me from selling a product to studying the acquisition process around it: how interest becomes a conversation, how a conversation becomes trust and how trust becomes revenue. I became more interested in the system around the sale than the transaction itself. That shift is what led me to study how incentives, information and technology shape commercial outcomes. chunks.title: Expanding my perspective — Perspective
chunks.text: Expanding my perspective Perspective 2023–present At the University of Ottawa, I study political science and economics alongside work. I chose the combination because it explains forces a sales floor cannot: why institutions behave the way they do, how incentives move groups and how societies trade off competing goods. The degree trained me to question assumptions, structure ambiguous problems and argue from evidence. It gave me a language for the strategic questions I was already asking at work. It connected the commercial world to the institutional and strategic questions behind it. I stopped seeing a business as a collection of functions and started seeing it as a set of choices. Research Critical thinking Economic reasoning Systems thinking Written communication Strategy University of Ottawa Political science and economics Research, analysis and strategy

chunks.title: Exploring business and technology — Business & Tech
chunks.text: Exploring business and technology Business & Tech 2025–present The next question was practical: how much of the repetitive work inside a business could be designed better? I started with AI agents and automation workflows, first as experiments and then as products. Working across H2Ops, Safiy and independent projects taught me to judge technology by operational fit, adoption and privacy, not novelty. I learned to move from a business problem to a process design, then to implementation — and to know when not to automate something. Technology became a way to act on commercial problems, not a separate identity. It added a third lens — what can actually be adopted and sustained — to the commercial and strategic ones. chunks.text: Where I’m heading Direction Present → next The common thread across these chapters is a shift in altitude: from one customer to a team, from a team to a market, from a market to the systems and incentives that shape it. Each step made me more useful at a different level of the business. My next step is consulting: helping organizations identify where strategy, operations and applied AI can create real value, then staying close enough to implementation to make the change work. Longer term, I want to lead and own businesses of my own — not for the title, but because the decisions I find most interesting are the ones that set direction for everyone else. chunks.title: About Nour
chunks.text: I'm based in Ottawa, studying political science and economics while working across sales, business systems and applied AI. The questions that hold my attention are usually about people and systems: why a customer says yes, why a team's behaviour changes when a target does, why some institutions adapt and others don't. Sales taught me to test those questions in conversation. Economics and political science gave me a language for the forces behind them. What I bring to an organization is a commercial read of the situation, the discipline to structure it, and enough technical fluency to turn the answer into something that runs.

chunks.title: How Nour thinks
chunks.text: I think in incentives and second-order effects. When someone presents a plan, I want to know what behaviour it rewards, what it assumes about people, and what happens after the first result. Psychology explains a lot of individual decisions; economics explains the trade-offs around them; politics explains why groups choose what they choose; philosophy keeps me honest about what better actually means. Technology is where those questions become testable. I'm comfortable holding an unresolved question longer than most people. I read, ask, compare cases, and change my mind when the evidence is better. Conviction without curiosity is just noise. The test I care about is whether an idea survives contact with real constraints — a budget, a customer, a team that has to use it on a Monday morning.

chunks.title: How Nour works
chunks.text: I start with the outcome and the constraint: what has to change, for whom, and what would make the change fail? Then I trace the work backwards from there. In practice that means customer conversations, messy data, process maps and a bias toward the smallest intervention that can prove something. I'd rather run a narrow test that produces evidence than defend a large plan that produces slides. I work best with people who care about the problem more than the org chart. I communicate plainly, take responsibility for the outcome, and adapt when the situation calls for it.

chunks.title: Nour direction
chunks.text: I want to work on problems where commercial judgment, business strategy and applied AI are all required — not as separate specialties, but as one way of thinking. The near-term direction is consulting or an operating role: understanding a business, finding where value is getting lost, and staying close enough to implementation to make the change real. Longer term, I want to lead — not for the title, but because the decisions I find most interesting are the ones that set direction for everyone else.

chunks.title: Career introduction
chunks.text: My career has moved through customers, commerce and systems, but the thread is a widening field of view: from a single sale to the systems that make sales repeatable, from a team’s performance to the incentives and technology behind it. Each chapter changed what I could see — and what I was useful for. Today I work where commercial judgment, business strategy and applied AI meet.
